claim: Adult skeletal muscle harbours a population of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) that are required for repair after tissue injury.
source: Adult skeletal muscle harbours a population of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) that are required for repair after tissue injury.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: In youth, MuSCs return to a reversible state of cell-cycle arrest termed 'quiescence' after injury resolution.
source: In youth, MuSCs return to a reversible state of cell-cycle arrest termed 'quiescence' after injury resolution.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MuSC behavior in young organisms.

claim: Some MuSCs in aged muscle remain semi-activated, causing a premature response to injuries that results in incomplete repair and eventual stem cell depletion.
source: Conversely, some MuSCs in aged muscle remain semi-activated, causing a premature response to injuries that results in incomplete repair and eventual stem cell depletion.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction and demonstrated experimentally in the manuscript.

claim: The mini-IDLE assay rapidly inactivates MuSCs freshly isolated from young murine skeletal muscle and returns them to a quiescent-like state for at least 1 week.
source: To fill this gap, we developed a simple and tractable in vitro method, to rapidly inactivate MuSCs freshly isolated from young murine skeletal muscle, and return them to a quiescent-like state for at least 1-week, which we name mini-IDLE (Inactivation and Dormancy LEveraged in vitro).
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by multiple experimental data points throughout the results section.

claim: The mini-IDLE assay is achieved by introducing MuSCs into a 3D bioartificial niche comprised of a thin sheet of mouse myotubes.
source: This was achieved by introducing MuSCs into a 3D bioartificial niche comprised of a thin sheet of mouse myotubes, which we demonstrate provides the minimal cues necessary to induce quiescence.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by data showing the necessity of 3D myotube culture.

claim: The mini-IDLE assay revealed cellular heterogeneity and population-level adaptations that converged on a common niche repopulation density.
source: With different starting numbers of MuSCs, the assay revealed cellular heterogeneity and population-level adaptations that converged on a common niche repopulation density; behaviours previously observed only in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 3.

claim: Quiescence-associated hallmarks in mini-IDLE included a Pax7+CalcR+DDX6+MyoD-c-FOS- signature.
source: Quiescence-associated hallmarks included a Pax7+CalcR+DDX6+MyoD-c-FOS- signature, quiescent-like morphologies, and polarized niche markers.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figures 3, 5, and supplementary figures.

claim: Quiescence-associated hallmarks in mini-IDLE included quiescent-like morphologies.
source: Quiescence-associated hallmarks included a Pax7+CalcR+DDX6+MyoD-c-FOS- signature, quiescent-like morphologies, and polarized niche markers.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Quiescence-associated hallmarks in mini-IDLE included polarized niche markers.
source: Quiescence-associated hallmarks included a Pax7+CalcR+DDX6+MyoD-c-FOS- signature, quiescent-like morphologies, and polarized niche markers.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 6.

claim: There is a relationship between morphology and cell fate signatures in MuSCs that enables real-time morphology-based screening.
source: Leveraging high-content bioimaging pipelines, we demonstrate a relationship between morphology and cell fate signatures for possible real-time morphology-based screening.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing correlation between morphological features and molecular markers.

claim: MuSCs from aged muscle displayed aberrant proliferative activities when introduced into mini-IDLE.
source: When using MuSCs from aged muscle, they displayed aberrant proliferative activities and delayed inactivation kinetics, among other quiescence-associated defects that we show are partially rescued by wortmannin treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: MuSCs from aged muscle displayed delayed inactivation kinetics when introduced into mini-IDLE.
source: When using MuSCs from aged muscle, they displayed aberrant proliferative activities and delayed inactivation kinetics, among other quiescence-associated defects that we show are partially rescued by wortmannin treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Quiescence-associated defects in aged MuSCs are partially rescued by wortmannin treatment.
source: When using MuSCs from aged muscle, they displayed aberrant proliferative activities and delayed inactivation kinetics, among other quiescence-associated defects that we show are partially rescued by wortmannin treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: MuSCs are identifiable by the selective expression of the paired-box transcription factor Pax7 in skeletal muscle tissue.
source: Muscle stem cells (MuSCs) are an adult stem cell population identifiable by the selective expression of the paired-box transcription factor Pax7 in skeletal muscle tissue, and are essential to muscle regeneration (Lepper et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2011; Sambasivan et al., 2011; Günther et al., 2013; von Maltzahn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: MuSCs are essential to muscle regeneration.
source: Muscle stem cells (MuSCs) are an adult stem cell population identifiable by the selective expression of the paired-box transcription factor Pax7 in skeletal muscle tissue, and are essential to muscle regeneration (Lepper et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2011; Sambasivan et al., 2011; Günther et al., 2013; von Maltzahn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: At rest, MuSCs exist in a reversible state of quiescence characterized by the absence of cell-cycle indicators.
source: At rest, MuSCs exist in a reversible state of quiescence characterized by, among other features, the absence of cell-cycle indicators (Chakkalakal et al., 2014; Cutler et al., 2022), lowered metabolic activity (Rocheteau et al., 2012) and RNA content (Machado et al., 2017), increased expression of genes such as CalcR, CD34, Spry-1, and Sdc4 (Machado et al., 2017; Pillon et al., 2020; Quarta et al., 2016), and revealed more recently – an elaborated morphology (Verma et al., 2018; Kann et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Quiescent MuSCs have lowered metabolic activity.
source: At rest, MuSCs exist in a reversible state of quiescence characterized by, among other features, the absence of cell-cycle indicators (Chakkalakal et al., 2014; Cutler et al., 2022), lowered metabolic activity (Rocheteau et al., 2012) and RNA content (Machado et al., 2017), increased expression of genes such as CalcR, CD34, Spry-1, and Sdc4 (Machado et al., 2017; Pillon et al., 2020; Quarta et al., 2016), and revealed more recently – an elaborated morphology (Verma et al., 2018; Kann et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Quiescent MuSCs have lowered RNA content.
source: At rest, MuSCs exist in a reversible state of quiescence characterized by, among other features, the absence of cell-cycle indicators (Chakkalakal et al., 2014; Cutler et al., 2022), lowered metabolic activity (Rocheteau et al., 2012) and RNA content (Machado et al., 2017), increased expression of genes such as CalcR, CD34, Spry-1, and Sdc4 (Machado et al., 2017; Pillon et al., 2020; Quarta et al., 2016), and revealed more recently – an elaborated morphology (Verma et al., 2018; Kann et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Quiescent MuSCs have increased expression of genes such as CalcR, CD34, Spry-1, and Sdc4.
source: At rest, MuSCs exist in a reversible state of quiescence characterized by, among other features, the absence of cell-cycle indicators (Chakkalakal et al., 2014; Cutler et al., 2022), lowered metabolic activity (Rocheteau et al., 2012) and RNA content (Machado et al., 2017), increased expression of genes such as CalcR, CD34, Spry-1, and Sdc4 (Machado et al., 2017; Pillon et al., 2020; Quarta et al., 2016), and revealed more recently – an elaborated morphology (Verma et al., 2018; Kann et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Quiescent MuSCs have an elaborated morphology.
source: At rest, MuSCs exist in a reversible state of quiescence characterized by, among other features, the absence of cell-cycle indicators (Chakkalakal et al., 2014; Cutler et al., 2022), lowered metabolic activity (Rocheteau et al., 2012) and RNA content (Machado et al., 2017), increased expression of genes such as CalcR, CD34, Spry-1, and Sdc4 (Machado et al., 2017; Pillon et al., 2020; Quarta et al., 2016), and revealed more recently – an elaborated morphology (Verma et al., 2018; Kann et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: MuSCs reside between a myofiber and the surrounding basal lamina.
source: Anatomically, they reside between a myofiber and the surrounding basal lamina, a highly specialized microenvironment or 'niche', that conveys unto them the popularized term 'satellite cell' (Mauro, 1961).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Quiescent MuSCs are constantly communicating with their niche.
source: Though quiescent, they are not dormant but are in fact idling; constantly communicating with their niche and waiting to respond to stressors (Van Velthoven and Rando, 2019; Crist et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MuSCs rapidly shift to an activated state in response to stressors such as physical activity, acute trauma, or myotoxic compounds.
source: Examples include significant physical activity causing mechanically induced damage, acute trauma, or exposure to myotoxic compounds that induce myofiber degradation (Baghdadi and Tajbakhsh, 2018; Murach et al., 2021). In these situations, MuSCs rapidly shift to an activated state wherein they enter cell cycle, and proliferate to produce progeny that differentiate to repair or create new myofibers, or they undertake self-renewing divisions where a subpopulation eventually returns to quiescence and repopulates the niche (Rudnicki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Quiescence is required for the long-term stability of the stem cell pool.
source: Quiescence is required for the long-term stability of the stem cell pool, and proper activation kinetics are necessary to ensure the integrity of the repair process (Ancel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Proper activation kinetics are necessary to ensure the integrity of the repair process.
source: Quiescence is required for the long-term stability of the stem cell pool, and proper activation kinetics are necessary to ensure the integrity of the repair process (Ancel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The depth of quiescence is positively correlated with stem cell potency.
source: The depth of quiescence is shown to be positively correlated with stem cell potency, or 'stemness'.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss of depth of quiescence in aging leads to less efficient and incomplete regeneration, and a progressive decline in MuSC number.
source: Indeed, instances where depth of quiescence is lost, such as in aging, leads to less efficient and incomplete regeneration, and a progressive decline in MuSC number (Chakkalakal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Tissue dissection, enzymatic digestion, and cell sorting impart an injury-associated stress response to MuSCs and cause isolation-induced activation.
source: This is because tissue dissection, enzymatic digestion, and cell sorting impart an injury-associated stress response to MuSCs, and cause isolation-induced activation (Machado et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Several studies describe in vitro approaches to delay activation for days by manipulating the culture substrate or media.
source: Several studies describe in vitro approaches to delay activation for days (at most) by manipulating the culture substrate or media (Charville et al., 2015; Arjona et al., 2022; Monge et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Combining a chemically defined 'quiescence media' with artificial muscle fibers maintained MuSCs in culture with limited proliferative activity for a 3.5-day period.
source: Alternatively, combining a chemically defined 'quiescence media' with artificial muscle fibers was reported to maintain MuSCs in culture with limited proliferative activity or changes to cell volume, and sustained CD34 expression for a 3.5-day period (Quarta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: 3D skeletal muscle macrotissue platforms support Pax7+ reserve cells within human myoblast populations to take on a reversible quiescent-like state.
source: More recently, three-dimensional (3D) skeletal muscle macrotissue platforms were shown to support Pax7+ reserve cells (Baroffio et al., 1996, Yoshida et al., 1998) within human myoblast populations to take on a reversible quiescent-like state (Tiburcy et al., 2019; Juhas et al., 2018; Fleming et al., 2020; Rajabian et al., 2021; Trevisan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: A strategy to inactivate freshly isolated adult MuSCs in culture for >3.5 days and to induce multiple molecular and morphological hallmarks of quiescence has not been reported prior to this study.
source: To date, a strategy to inactivate freshly isolated adult MuSCs in culture for >3.5 days and to induce multiple molecular and morphological hallmarks of quiescence has yet to be reported.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current work based on review of existing literature.

claim: Peak myotube content (≈65% by sarcomeric α-actinin tissue coverage) and a nuclear fusion index of 90% was achieved by 5 days in differentiation media with as few as 25,000 cells per tissue.
source: Peak myotube content (≈65% by sarcomeric α-actinin (SAA) tissue coverage) and a nuclear fusion index of 90% was achieved by 5 days in DM with as few as 25,000 cells per tissue (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mitochondrial activity was significantly reduced on day 18 when compared to day 10 of myotube template culture.
source: A colorimetric metabolic activity assay (i.e. MTS) revealed that mitochondrial activity was significantly reduced on day 18 when compared to day 10 (Figure 1E), another indication that the integrity of the tissues becomes compromised at later timepoints.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Day 5 to day 14 of myotube template culture serves as the assay window.
source: Based on these analyses, we established conditions to engineer a mouse myotube template and concluded that day 5 to day 14 of myotube template culture would serve as the assay window.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: By day 12, 2D myotube cultures showed detachment zones which translated to a significant drop in SAA coverage compared to 3D myotube templates.
source: Specifically, by day 12 we observed detachment zones in 2D cultures which translated to a significant drop in SAA coverage compared to our 3D myotube templates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 2D myotube cultures showed a higher incidence of multinucleated, SAA+ sphere-shaped structures indicative of retracted myotubes.
source: Upon closer inspection, we also observed a higher incidence of multinucleated, SAA+ sphere-shaped structures, indicative of retracted myotubes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The proportion of striations per field of view is increased in 3D myotube culture at the day 5 timepoint compared to 2D culture.
source: According to the Z-line fraction (i.e. the fraction of SAA skeleton classified as Z-lines by actin guided segmentation), the proportion of striations per field of view is increased in 3D at the day 5 timepoint, with 2D cultures eventually catching up by day 8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Mean sarcomere length is increased in 3D myotube culture compared to 2D culture.
source: While we noted no differences in mean continuous Z-line length, we found an increase in mean sarcomere length in 3D culture, which is closer to the length-tension plateau reported in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G; Moo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claim: 3D myotube templates show little to no myotube detachment over 12 days of differentiation.
source: Thus, by contrast to 2D culture, 3D myotube templates show little to no myotube detachment over 12 days of differentiation and a quicker obtention of striations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: An average purity of 93% Pax7+ cells was achieved using the MACS protocol.
source: By conducting two rounds of microbead-based lineage depletion followed by integrin α-7 enrichment, we achieved an average purity of 93% Pax7+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which meets FACS purity values reported by others (Maesner et al., 2016; Kuang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over the 1-week culture period, the Pax7+ mononuclear donor cells were distributed throughout the myotube template and adopted an elongated morphology that aligned with the local myotubes.
source: Over the 1-week culture period, the Pax7+ mononuclear donor (YFP+) cells were seen distributed throughout the myotube template and adopting an elongated morphology that aligned with the local myotubes (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Seeding 500 MuSCs resulted in a relatively stable pool size over time.
source: Seeding 500 MuSCs resulted in a relatively stable pool size over time.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: When a higher (1500 or 2500) or lower number of MuSCs were introduced to myotube templates, over time the number of Pax7+ donor cells converged to match the pool size attained in the 500 MuSC condition.
source: Interestingly, when a higher (1500 or 2500) or lower number of MuSCs were introduced to myotube templates, over time the number of Pax7+ donor cells converged to match the pool size attained in the 500 MuSC condition (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The engrafted MuSC population persists and establishes a steady-state cell density within the engineered niche.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the engrafted MuSC population persists and establishes a steady-state cell density within the engineered niche.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: CalcR is expressed by quiescent MuSCs but is absent from all MuSCs within 48 hr of an in vivo myotoxin injury or within 48 hr of prospective isolation followed by in vitro culture.
source: Indeed, at the protein level, CalcR is expressed by quiescent MuSCs, but is then absent from all MuSCs within 48 hr of an in vivo myotoxin injury or within 48 hr of prospective isolation followed by in vitro culture (Yamaguchi et al., 2015; Baghdadi et al., 2018; Gnocchi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The majority of MuSCs expressed CalcR at 1 DPE, with a sharp decline in the proportion of CalcR+ donor cells observed at 3 DPE.
source: In the context of our 3D culture assay, the majority of MuSCs expressed CalcR at 1 DPE, with a sharp decline in the proportion of CalcR+ donor cells observed at 3 DPE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ~15% of donor MuSCs were CalcR+ at both 3 and 7 DPE.
source: Interestingly, ~15% of donor MuSCs were CalcR+ at both 3 and 7 DPE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ≈75% of the donor MuSCs engrafted within the myotube templates expressed c-FOS after a single day of culture.
source: After a single day of culture, we found that ≈75% of the donor MuSCs (YFP+caveolin-1+ cells) engrafted within the myotube templates expressed the transcription factor c-FOS, among the earliest transcriptional events reported to date in the MuSC activation sequence (Machado et al., 2017; Almada et al., 2021; Yue et al., 2020; van Velthoven et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: By 3 DPE, the proportion of caveolin-1+c-FOS+ mononuclear cells dropped to ≈30%, with similar proportions observed on 7 DPE.
source: By 3 DPE, the proportion of caveolin-1+c-FOS+ mononuclear cells dropped to ≈30%, with similar proportions observed on 7 DPE (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The maintenance of a steady-state population of donor MuSCs from 1 to 3 DPE, coupled with the rapid loss of c-FOS immunolabelling by 3 DPE, suggests that myotube template culture induces MuSCs to inactivate.
source: The maintenance of a steady-state population of donor MuSCs from 1 to 3 DPE, coupled with the rapid loss of c-FOS immunolabelling by 3 DPE, suggests that myotube template culture induces MuSCs to inactivate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: At 3 DPE, only ≈1/3 of the Pax7+ mononuclear donor cell population was Ki67+, and this dropped to ≈10% by 7 DPE.
source: Consistently, when we quantified the incidence of MuSCs in the active phase of the cell cycle via Ki67 labelling, we found that at 3 DPE, only ≈1/3 of the Pax7+ mononuclear donor cell population was Ki67+, and this dropped to ≈10% by 7 DPE (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Of the Ki67- mononuclear donor cells present at 7 DPE, the vast majority were EdU-.
source: Of the Ki67- mononuclear donor cells present at 7 DPE, the vast majority were EdU- (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Approximately 30% of Ki67- mononuclear donor cells at 7 DPE were EdU+, indicating cell-cycle entry at some point during the 1-week culture period, and a cessation by 7 DPE.
source: Approximately 30% were EdU+, indicating cell-cycle entry at some point during the 1-week culture period, and a cessation by 7 DPE (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The main fate of the EdU labelled MuSCs is eventual cell-cycle exit, and not myotube fusion.
source: This data, together with a scarcity of EdU+ myonuclei observed in the cultures (data not shown), suggests that the main fate of the EdU labelled MuSCs is eventual cell-cycle exit, and not myotube fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the EdU/Ki67 data and observation of EdU+ myonuclei.

claim: Barium chloride exposure induced effective clearing of the myotubes with a non-significant change to MuSC population density.
source: We first established a barium chloride exposure protocol that induced effective clearing of the myotubes with a non-significant change to MuSC population density (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A statistically significant increase in the proportion of Ki67+ cells was observed 2 days post-injury compared to the control condition.
source: We then analysed the mononuclear YFP+Pax7+ population 2 days post-injury and observed a statistically significant increase in the proportion of Ki67+ cells as compared to the control condition (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Myotube template cultures allow for inactivation and cell-cycle exit of engrafted MuSCs, which can be reversed with the injury-associated stimuli caused by barium chloride exposure.
source: Thus, myotube template cultures allow for inactivation and cell-cycle exit of engrafted MuSCs, which can be reversed with the injury-associated stimuli caused by barium chloride exposure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Compared with the 500 MuSC seeding condition, there was a significant increase in the proportion of mononuclear YFP+Ki67- cells that were EdU+ at 7 DPE in cultures seeded with 200 MuSCs.
source: Compared with the 500 MuSC seeding condition, we found a significant increase in the proportion of mononuclear YFP+Ki67- cells that were EdU+ at 7 DPE in cultures seeded with 200 MuSCs, suggesting the MuSC pool expanded to attain a steady-state density (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: In conditions where >500 MuSCs were seeded, a significant decrease in the proportion of mononuclear YFP+Ki67- cells that were EdU+ at 7 DPE was observed.
source: By contrast, in conditions where >500 MuSCs were seeded, a significant decrease in the proportion of mononuclear YFP+Ki67- cells that were EdU+ at 7 DPE was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: A qualitatively greater number of donor-derived myotubes was observed in cultures seeded with >500 MuSCs.
source: Consistent with the latter hypothesis, upon visual inspection we saw a qualitatively greater number of donor-derived myotubes in the cultures seeded with >500 MuSCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), which was confirmed by quantifying the percentage area of myotube templates covered by YFP signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: MuSCs meet a steady-state population density via increased proliferation when beginning below the 500 cell threshold, and with increased cell fusion when beginning above it.
source: In sum, we conclude that MuSCs meet a steady-state population density via increased proliferation when beginning below the 500 cell threshold, and with increased cell fusion when beginning above it.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: MuSCs seeded onto tissues on day 0 of myotube template differentiation resulted in a progressive loss of YFP+Pax7+ mononuclear cells.
source: Compared to MuSCs seeded on myotube templates on day 5 of differentiation, day 0 seeding resulted in a progressive loss of YFP+Pax7+ mononuclear cells, and most of those that remained were Ki67+ (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The striking contrast in YFP+ myotube content observed at 7 DPE upon comparing day 0 and day 5 seeding conditions suggests that the MuSCs engrafted on day 0 had undergone differentiation.
source: The striking contrast in YFP+ myotube content observed at 7 DPE upon comparing these two conditions suggests that the MuSCs engrafted on day 0 had undergone differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 3D cellulose-reinforced hydrogel alone was not sufficient to support MuSC inactivation and maintenance.
source: However, this notion was abandoned upon finding that the outcome of this culture scenario (Figure 4E) very closely matched what we observed when the MuSCs were cultured in 2D Geltrex-coated culture wells (Figure 4B); a loss of the YFP+Pax7+ mononuclear population over time.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Upon adding MuSCs to a day 5 monolayer of myotubes in 2D culture, a Pax7+ population was maintained over the 1-week culture period.
source: Indeed, upon adding MuSCs to a day 5 monolayer of myotubes in 2D culture, a Pax7+ population was maintained over the 1-week culture period (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In 2D myotube culture, only a minority of the Pax7+ donor cells were Ki67- at 7 DPE.
source: But in striking contrast to the 3D myotube template culture (Figure 4C), only a minority of the Pax7+ donor cells were Ki67- at 7 DPE (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Myotubes are necessary for Pax7+ MuSC persistence.
source: From this iterative analysis, we conclude that myotubes are necessary for Pax7+ MuSC persistence, and that the combination of myotubes and a 3D culture environment drives the MuSC inactivation process.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The combination of myotubes and a 3D culture environment drives the MuSC inactivation process.
source: From this iterative analysis, we conclude that myotubes are necessary for Pax7+ MuSC persistence, and that the combination of myotubes and a 3D culture environment drives the MuSC inactivation process.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The Pax7+ donor cell population progressively shifted from low max/min Feret diameter ratios and eccentricities to high max/min Feret diameter ratios and eccentricities over time in 3D myotube culture.
source: With this pipeline, we determined that the Pax7+ donor cell population progressively shifted from low max/min Feret diameter ratios and eccentricities (lower left quadrant) to high max/min Feret diameter ratios and eccentricities (upper right quadrant) over time in 3D myotube culture (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Quiescence-associated morphologies were most prominent in the context of the 3D engineered niche.
source: By conducting a side-by-side comparison of these features when MuSCs were cultured in 2D culture, vs. amongst a 2D myotube monolayer or within the 3D myotube template, we concluded that quiescence-associated morphologies were most prominent in the context of the 3D engineered niche (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: DDX6+ puncta progressively accumulate within MuSCs cultured in the 3D in vitro assay.
source: Consistently, DDX6+ puncta progressively accumulate within MuSCs cultured in the 3D in vitro assay (Figure 5D–E), and we report a significant linear trend increase between the morphology of the cells and the number of DDX6+ puncta at 7 DPE (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There is a significant linear trend increase between the morphology of the cells and the number of DDX6+ puncta at 7 DPE.
source: Consistently, DDX6+ puncta progressively accumulate within MuSCs cultured in the 3D in vitro assay (Figure 5D–E), and we report a significant linear trend increase between the morphology of the cells and the number of DDX6+ puncta at 7 DPE (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Nuclear eccentricity differs between Pax7+MyoD+ and Pax7+MyoD- populations by 3 DPE.
source: By evaluating the mean max/min Feret diameter ratio and mean eccentricity values of the Pax7+MyoD+ and Pax7+MyoD- cell populations, we found that nuclear eccentricity differs between the populations by 3 DPE, while population divergence according to max/min Feret diameter ratio (˃2-fold) emerged a bit later, at 7 DPE (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Population divergence according to max/min Feret diameter ratio (˃2-fold) emerged at 7 DPE.
source: By evaluating the mean max/min Feret diameter ratio and mean eccentricity values of the Pax7+MyoD+ and Pax7+MyoD- cell populations, we found that nuclear eccentricity differs between the populations by 3 DPE, while population divergence according to max/min Feret diameter ratio (˃2-fold) emerged a bit later, at 7 DPE (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Nuclear morphology of the Pax7+MyoD- population showed a progressive, statistically significant transition to a rice-like shape.
source: Specifically, nuclear morphology of the Pax7+MyoD- population showed a progressive, statistically significant transition to a rice-like shape, while Pax7+MyoD+ nuclei remained more rounded.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Elongation of the cell body and elaborate projections were features that exclusively characterized the Pax7+MyoD- cell population, and emerged between 3 and 7 DPE.
source: Elongation of the cell body and elaborate projections were features that exclusively characterized the Pax7+MyoD- cell population, and emerged between 3 and 7 DPE.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Donor cells with a max/min Feret diameter ≥5.8 uniformly displayed the Pax7+MyoD- signature of inactivated cells.
source: Indeed, donor cells with a max/min Feret diameter ≥5.8 uniformly displayed the Pax7+MyoD- signature of inactivated cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Y-27632 treatment did not result in a significant shift in Pax7+ cell population-level kinetics.
source: The treatment did not result in a significant shift in Pax7+ cell population-level kinetics (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–B), and while c-FOS labelling showed a trending decrease in c-FOS+ cells at 3 DPE, it was not significant (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4B.

claim: MyoD labelling revealed a Y-27632-induced block on the acquisition of a transiently activated subpopulation of MuSCs as had been observed in the control conditions at 3 DPE.
source: However, MyoD labelling revealed a Y-27632-induced block on the acquisition of a transiently activated subpopulation of MuSCs as had been observed in the control conditions at 3 DPE (Figure 5—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Y-27632 treatment caused a shift towards the elongated morphology of quiescent-like cells at 3 DPE that was not attained in the control condition until 7 DPE.
source: Specifically, our evaluations of the max/min Feret diameter ratios of MuSCs indicated that Y-27632 treatment caused a shift towards the elongated morphology of quiescent-like cells at 3 DPE that was not attained in the control condition until 7 DPE.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Y-27632 treatment appeared to hasten the process of inactivation and the acquisition of a quiescent-like morphology.
source: Thus, the Y-27632 treatment appeared to hasten the process of inactivation and, also, the acquisition of a quiescent-like morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and 5.

claim: Y-27632 treatment elicited a significant influence over the morphology of the Pax7+MyoD+ population.
source: From this, we observed that the Y-27632 treatment elicited a significant influence over the morphology of the Pax7+MyoD+ population, which in some cases (e.g. nuclear eccentricity, branching), matched, but did not supersede, the quiescent-like morphology of the Pax7+MyoD- engrafted cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The progression of the Pax7+MyoD- population towards a quiescent-like morphology appeared to be uninfluenced by the Y-27632 treatment when compared against the control.
source: By contrast, the progression of the Pax7+MyoD- population towards a quiescent-like morphology appeared to be uninfluenced by the Y-27632 treatment when compared against the control.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Y-27632 treatment increased the proportion of inactivated (c-Fos-Pax7+MyoD-) MuSCs at 3DPE.
source: Thus, Y-27632 treatment increased the proportion of inactivated (c-Fos-Pax7+MyoD-) MuSCs at 3DPE, which progressed to a quiescent-like morphology in a Y-27632 agnostic manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and 5.

claim: Y-27632 treatment coaxed the Pax7+MyoD+ population to acquire quiescence-associated morphologies.
source: In parallel, Y-27632 treatment coaxed the Pax7+MyoD+ population to acquire quiescence-associated morphologies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Changes in nuclear morphology precede cell body extension and establishment of quiescent-like projections during the inactivation process.
source: Taken together, morphological analysis of the engrafted MuSCs suggests that changes in nuclear morphology precede cell body extension and establishment of quiescent-like projections during the inactivation process, that morphometric features alone may predict MuSC inactivation status, and offers further support that cytoskeletal remodelling through Rho family GTPase signalling dictates the MuSC transition between activation and quiescence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Morphometric features alone may predict MuSC inactivation status.
source: Taken together, morphological analysis of the engrafted MuSCs suggests that changes in nuclear morphology precede cell body extension and establishment of quiescent-like projections during the inactivation process, that morphometric features alone may predict MuSC inactivation status, and offers further support that cytoskeletal remodelling through Rho family GTPase signalling dictates the MuSC transition between activation and quiescence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Cytoskeletal remodelling through Rho family GTPase signalling dictates the MuSC transition between activation and quiescence.
source: Taken together, morphological analysis of the engrafted MuSCs suggests that changes in nuclear morphology precede cell body extension and establishment of quiescent-like projections during the inactivation process, that morphometric features alone may predict MuSC inactivation status, and offers further support that cytoskeletal remodelling through Rho family GTPase signalling dictates the MuSC transition between activation and quiescence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5 and supplementary figures, and supported by citations.

claim: For more than two-thirds of donor cells, M-cadherin expression restricted to the apical interface was observed at 7 DPE.
source: By evaluating immunolabelled tissues at 7 DPE, we found that most mononucleated donor cells had an elongated morphology and were closely associated with multinucleated myotubes. For more than two-thirds of donor cells, M-cadherin expression restricted to the apical interface was observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Quiescent MuSCs localize the N-cadherin adhesion molecule to the tips of elaborated cytoplasmic projections.
source: It was recently discovered that quiescent MuSCs localize the N-cadherin adhesion molecule to the tips of elaborated cytoplasmic projections (coined 'quiescent projections') (Kann et al., 2022), a feature we also observed within our culture assay at 7 DPE (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and confirmed by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: N-cadherin+ cytoplasmic projections were found in ≈45% of mononuclear donor cells at 7 DPE.
source: Examples such as these were found in ≈45% of mononuclear donor cells (Figure 6C), and in each case the Pax7+ donor cell morphology was characterized by a long oval-shaped nucleus and very long, elaborated cytoplasmic projections.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Examples of polarized distribution of M-cadherin and integrin α-7 or laminin α-2 in Pax7+ donor cells were identified, albeit with lower frequency.
source: Furthermore, we identified examples of polarized distribution of M-cadherin and integrin α-7 or laminin α-2 in Pax7+ donor cells, albeit with lower frequency (Figure 6B and D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D and images in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The engrafted MuSCs can recapitulate anatomical hallmarks of MuSCs residing within adult homeostatic skeletal muscle.
source: This evidence demonstrates that the engrafted MuSCs can recapitulate anatomical hallmarks of MuSCs residing within adult homeostatic skeletal muscle, and suggests that acquisition of these features is dependent on interactions with MuSCs and their immediate myofiber niche.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Acquisition of anatomical hallmarks is dependent on interactions with MuSCs and their immediate myofiber niche.
source: This evidence demonstrates that the engrafted MuSCs can recapitulate anatomical hallmarks of MuSCs residing within adult homeostatic skeletal muscle, and suggests that acquisition of these features is dependent on interactions with MuSCs and their immediate myofiber niche.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Upon seeding 500 MuSCs isolated from aged muscle onto a young 3D myotube template, an ≈2-fold increase in Pax7+ mononucleated donor cell density was quantified by 3 DPE relative to tissues engrafted by young MuSCs.
source: Upon seeding 500 MuSCs isolated from aged muscle onto a young 3D myotube template, we quantified an ≈2-fold increase in Pax7+ mononucleated donor cell density by 3 DPE relative to tissues engrafted by young MuSCs and analysed at the same timepoint (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A greater proportion of aged as compared to young MuSCs were Ki67+ at 3 DPE.
source: Consistently, a greater proportion of aged as compared to young MuSCs were Ki67+ at 3 DPE, and aged MuSC morphology at this timepoint diverged significantly from that observed of young MuSCs in 3D myotube cultures (Figure 7B–C and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Aged MuSC morphology at 3 DPE diverged significantly from that observed of young MuSCs in 3D myotube cultures.
source: Consistently, a greater proportion of aged as compared to young MuSCs were Ki67+ at 3 DPE, and aged MuSC morphology at this timepoint diverged significantly from that observed of young MuSCs in 3D myotube cultures (Figure 7B–C and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: By 7 DPE, aged MuSC engrafted cultures showed a small, but significant, decrease in population density compared to young MuSC engrafted tissues.
source: By 7 DPE, aged MuSC engrafted cultures showed a small, but significant, decrease in population density compared to young MuSC engrafted tissues (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The aged MuSCs were unable to maintain pool size and the production of Pax7+ donor cells observed at 3 DPE culminated in differentiation to myotubes.
source: This, coupled with the trending increase in donor cell GFP+ signal covering tissues at this timepoint (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), suggested that the aged MuSCs were unable to maintain pool size and that the production of Pax7+ donor cells observed at 3 DPE culminated in differentiation to myotubes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mononucleated aged Pax7+ donor cell population showed a decline in the proportion of c-FOS+ and Ki67+ cells with time, albeit with delayed inactivation kinetics when compared to young MuSCs.
source: Nonetheless, the mononucleated aged Pax7+ donor cell population that persisted throughout the culture period showed a decline in the proportion of c-FOS+ (Figure 7D) and Ki67+ (Figure 7C) cells with time, albeit with delayed inactivation kinetics when compared to young MuSCs (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: On average, aged donor cells had reduced max/min Feret diameter ratio and nuclear eccentricity when compared to young cells at 7 DPE.
source: On average, aged donor cells had reduced max/min Feret diameter ratio and nuclear eccentricity when compared to young cells at this timepoint, which correlates to the more contracted/rounded morphological characteristics of activated MuSCs (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: Compared to young MuSCs, aged MuSCs presented increased proliferation and reduced FoxO3a nuclear fluorescent intensity in 2D culture.
source: First, we confirmed that compared to young MuSCs, aged MuSCs presented increased proliferation and reduced FoxO3a nuclear fluorescent intensity in 2D culture.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Wortmannin treatment (10 µM) blunted cell proliferation and increased FoxO3a nuclear localization in both young and aged MuSCs in 2D culture.
source: In this context, wortmannin treatment (10 µM) blunted cell proliferation and increased FoxO3a nuclear localization in both young and aged MuSCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: FoxO3a nuclear fluorescent intensity was comparable between young and aged MuSCs following wortmannin treatment in 2D culture.
source: Indeed, FoxO3a nuclear fluorescent intensity was comparable between young and aged MuSCs following wortmannin treatment in 2D culture (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: With wortmannin treatment, the aged MuSCs maintained a stable Pax7+ donor population over time, that was indistinguishable from the untreated young MuSCs cultures.
source: With this treatment, the aged MuSCs maintained a stable Pax7+ donor population over time, that was indistinguishable from the untreated young MuSCs cultures (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: The proportions of Ki67+ and c-FOS+ in the aged Pax7+ population showed comparable kinetics to the young untreated donor MuSCs with wortmannin treatment.
source: Indeed, the proportions of Ki67+ and c-FOS+ in the aged Pax7+ population showed comparable kinetics to the young untreated donor MuSCs (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Wortmannin treatment encouraged a greater proportion of young MuSCs to inactivate, and with more rapid kinetics.
source: As well, the treatment encouraged a greater proportion of young MuSCs to inactivate, and with more rapid kinetics (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: There was a trending decrease in donor cell GFP+ signal covering tissues at 7 DPE in wortmannin-treated conditions, suggesting reduced differentiation.
source: We also found a trending decrease in donor cell GFP+ signal covering tissues at 7 DPE in wortmannin-treated conditions, suggesting reduced differentiation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Morphological characterization of wortmannin-treated aged MuSCs at 7 DPE showed no change in average max/min Feret diameter ratio.
source: Finally, morphological characterization of wortmannin-treated aged MuSCs at 7 DPE showed no change in average max/min Feret diameter ratio, whereas we found a rescue of nuclear eccentricity that matched young MuSCs (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: Wortmannin treatment rescued nuclear eccentricity in aged MuSCs at 7 DPE that matched young MuSCs.
source: Finally, morphological characterization of wortmannin-treated aged MuSCs at 7 DPE showed no change in average max/min Feret diameter ratio, whereas we found a rescue of nuclear eccentricity that matched young MuSCs (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: There were no shifts in the morphological profile of young MuSCs treated with wortmannin.
source: There were no shifts in the morphological profile of young MuSCs treated with wortmannin (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: By introducing aged MuSCs into a young myotube niche, abnormal population maintenance, delays in the inactivation kinetics, and morphological features characteristic of activated MuSCs were revealed.
source: Thus, by introducing aged MuSCs into a young myotube niche we revealed abnormal population maintenance, delays in the inactivation kinetics, and morphological features characteristic of activated MuSCs, which we show can be dampened by modulating AKT signalling in the context of the mini-IDLE assay.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Abnormal population maintenance, delays in the inactivation kinetics, and morphological features characteristic of activated MuSCs in aged MuSCs can be dampened by modulating AKT signalling in the context of the mini-IDLE assay.
source: Thus, by introducing aged MuSCs into a young myotube niche we revealed abnormal population maintenance, delays in the inactivation kinetics, and morphological features characteristic of activated MuSCs, which we show can be dampened by modulating AKT signalling in the context of the mini-IDLE assay.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The mini-IDLE assay is a culture assay capable of recapitulating aspects of quiescent mouse MuSC biology, in youth and in age, that were previously not possible to study in vitro.
source: To conclude, herein we report that mini-IDLE is a culture assay capable of recapitulating aspects of quiescent mouse MuSC biology, in youth and in age, that were previously not possible to study in vitro.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: The mini-IDLE method is modular, allowing introduction and even distribution of new cellular components to the assay at any time-point.
source: By contrast to all other 3D culture systems where the cellular and ECM components are mixed together and introduced at the start of the experiment (Tiburcy et al., 2019; Fleming et al., 2020; Rajabian et al., 2021; Trevisan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022a; Afshar Bakooshli et al., 2019; Madden et al., 2015; Afshar et al., 2020), our method is modular. Amongst the merits of this distinction is the ability to introduce and evenly distribute new cellular components to the assay at any time-point.
evidence: This is a description of the method and its advantages.

claim: It is feasible to genetically modify the MuSC and myoblast components in different ways, and maintain these distinctions, when MuSCs are introduced to the muscle tissue after myotubes have formed.
source: It is also feasible to genetically modify the MuSC and myoblast components in different ways, and maintain these distinctions, when MuSCs are introduced to the muscle tissue after myotubes have formed.
evidence: This is a description of the method and its advantages.
